contentHtml:
As India’s elderly population grows, the focus of senior care needs to move beyond housing to an integrated ecosystem that ensures continuity of care, dignity and quality of life. Neha Sinha, Dementia Specialist & Clinical Psychologist, CEO and Co-Founder, Epoch Elder Care, discusses the way forward

India is aging faster than the systems built to look after its elders, and the Association of Senior Living India’s Silver Surge 2.0 report doesn’t shy away from saying so. For years the sector has measured progress in homes built. The harder question now is how well we support the people living in them, day after day.

What we mean by a care ecosystem

Care is part of it, of course. When we talk about an ecosystem, though, we mean everything around an elder that keeps their life going as it changes: their health, yes, but also their moods, their friends, their faith and the small routines that make a day feel like their own. Nobody should have to trade one of these away to hold on to another.

Look at how elder care in India has developed and you can trace a fairly clear line. All solutions used to work in silos such as ”home care” ”active ageing” ”assisted living” ”nursing care” recovery or transition care. Ecosystems are where that line points next. The goal is a life that feels as ordinary as possible, which sounds modest until you actually try to deliver it. It takes compassion and a great deal of patient work, and that is exactly what the ASLI report argues for.

Later life rarely narrows in one direction at a time. A person can be perfectly fit and still lonely. Someone else might keep a busy social life yet miss the morning puja or weekly temple visit that used to give the week its shape. Treating these as separate service lines misses the point, since they all belong to one person. When independence, belonging, purpose and comfort are looked after together, a building begins to feel like home.

Where things stand today

Much of India’s organised elder care is now run by a small number of private operators. They started out when there was hardly a market, did a lot of the groundwork themselves, and have earned families’ trust over time. The demographics show why that trust is building so quickly. The report puts India’s 60-plus population at 166.9 million in 2026, rising to 191.5 million by 2030 and around 347 million by 2050. It’s easy to read these as statistics. They’re really our parents and neighbours, and the uncle down the road.

Providers feel the change too. In the PwC–ASLI survey, 84 per cent said they were highly optimistic about growth over the next 15 years, and the same share saw wider acceptance of senior care services as the main reason. About 63 per cent pointed to families being more aware of what’s available. On the supply side, organised senior care has grown at 14.2 per cent a year since 2024. Families have changed as well. They come to us better informed and more open to organised care than they used to be. The old idea that care can only happen at home or the concept of an ‘’old age home’’ is being rethought, usually out of love and not because anyone has given up. Many families find that bringing in professional help brings them closer to their parents, because the relationship no longer revolves around caregiving alone.

Why the ecosystem matters as much as the home

Housing answers the question of where an elder lives today. The ecosystem deals with a more anxious one: what happens later? Families need an answer to both. Mental health is the biggest blind spot. It tends to get pushed behind physical safety, when engagement, emotional support and a sense of purpose are what make the rest of a care plan worth following in the first place.

At 70 and beyond, when the right care is not available, it is often replaced by a far more drastic alternative: hospitalisation. According to the study, one in eight older adults (12.2 per cent) has supportive or palliative care needs, and elders aged 70+ are hospitalised at more than four times the rate of adults aged 30-44. These figures show that where everyday, preventive care is absent, the health system ends up absorbing the cost, and the elder bears the disruption.

Then there’s continuity. Good support adjusts along the way. Families should be kept in the loop the whole time, so that a son working in another city feels as reassured as a daughter who lives ten minutes away. This is why we think the sector’s focus has to shift from buildings to relationships, and from individual services to continuity. What an elder really wants from a community is the promise that they’ll be understood and supported at every stage.

The gaps we still need to close

Policy. Government frameworks for elder care are beginning to take shape and a few measures are already in place, which is encouraging. They need to go further, and they should be designed with the people who’d benefit most in mind, particularly those over 65, when needs usually become more complex and options start to shrink. Policy should match the elder population India has now. Much of what exists was written for the one we expected a generation ago.

Access. Access not only to care, but care that is best suited for each elder. Assisted living accounts for less than 10% of organised senior living stock in India, compared with 24-29 per cent in mature markets. Operators expect memory care to emerge as the leading area of specialisation, alongside continuum-of-care communities.

Affordability. Quality care shouldn’t be a privilege for a few families. Getting there means sensible pricing, standards that don’t slip and an honest look at what Indian households can actually manage. Nobody is asking for diluted care, only for models that more families can keep up with while keeping their dignity.

Movement on one of these won’t count for much without the others. A strong policy does nothing for a family that can’t reach or pay for the service, and a well-priced service that exists in a handful of cities only goes so far.

Building it together

While we steadily build this ecosystem, we must ensure that it holds our elders in the highest regard. Behind every statistic, we see a lifetime of lived experiences of an elder, and the people who care for them, our caregivers, deserve the same dignity and support. This is not an abstract ambition. It is the daily responsibility of earning an elder’s trust and a family’s confidence.

Success is not measured in occupancy or the size of a community. It is measured in whether an elder wakes up feeling at home, cared for with compassion and expertise, among people who know their story and their preferences. It is measured in whether that elder can trust that, whatever comes next, they will be looked after without having to give up the life they love. Building the care, continuity and belonging that fills a home matters as much as the home, and it is work that we must be willing to measure, share and be held accountable for. Housing gives us the foundation. The ecosystem is what makes it worth building on.
